meta.title: Ten Days That Shook the World: places, factions and movements in Reed's Petrograd

blocs.soviet: For the insurrection and Soviet power: the Bolsheviki, the Left SRs, the Military Revolutionary Committee, the Red Guards, most of the garrison and the fleet.
blocs.government: The Provisional Government and those who fought for it: its ministers and staff, the yunker schools, Krasnov's Cossacks, the Women's Battalion.
blocs.opposition: Against the insurrection without being the deposed government: the City Duma, the Committee for Salvation, the Mensheviki and SRs, the Cadets, the old Tsay-ee-kah and Peasants' Executive.
blocs.neutral: Declared neutral or split: the Petrograd Cossacks, Vikzhel, several regiments.

days.label: 4 Nov
days.name: The Day of the Petrograd Soviet

days.label: 7 Nov
days.name: The fall of the Provisional Government

days.label: 13 Nov
days.name: First snow; out to the front

avrora-anchorage.name: The Avrora’s anchorage in the Neva
avrora-anchorage.ident: Reed (App. IV) has the cruiser “anchored in the Neva”. Her commissar’s report puts the anchorage “near the Nikolaevskii Bridge”; the pin is a guess within that.

cirque-moderne.name: Cirque Moderne
cirque-moderne.ident: Reed goes “across the river” to it; it stood on Kronverksky Prospekt on the Petrograd Side. The exact site is not verified, hence the wide radius.

city-duma.name: City Duma
city-duma.note: The Alexander Hall and the Nicolai Hall were inside. Seat of the Committee for Salvation from 8 Nov.

engineers-castle.name: Engineers’ Castle (Nikolaevsky Engineering School)
engineers-castle.ident: Reed’s “Injinierny Zamok”, the School of Engineers, housed in the Mikhailovsky Castle.

finland-station.name: Finland Station
finland-station.today: Rebuilt in 1960; one fragment of the old front survives.

fontanka-6.name: Imperial School of Jurisprudence, Fontanka 6
fontanka-6.note: Seat of the Executive Committee of the Peasants’ Soviets; the peasants’ procession set out from here on 29 Nov.

foreign-ministry.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs (east wing of the General Staff building)
foreign-ministry.ident: The ministry occupied the east wing of the General Staff building, on the Moika.

general-staff.name: General Staff building (Petrograd Military District Staff)
general-staff.ident: Reed’s “great red building of the General Staff” and “Petrograd Staff Headquarters”: the Military District staff sat in the General Staff building. Its OSM element covers only the west wing, Palace Square 10, up to the arch; the east wing beyond the arch is mapped separately.

gogol-corner.name: Corner of Gogol Street (Malaya Morskaya) and St Isaac’s Square
gogol-corner.ru: Угол Малой Морской и Исаакиевской площади
gogol-corner.ident: Malaya Morskaya was named Gogol Street from 1902. The car came “from the Admiralty, on its way to the Telephone Exchange”, so the pin is where Gogol Street leaves the north-east corner of St Isaac’s Square; which corner Bryant meant is not certain.

grebetskaya-corner.name: Corner of the Grebetskaya and the Bolshoy Prospekt
grebetskaya-corner.ident: Bolshaya Grebetskaya is now Pionerskaya Street; it meets the Bolshoy Prospekt of the Petrograd Side.
grebetskaya-corner.reed: corner of the Grebetskaya and the Bolshoy Prospekt

hotel-france.name: Hotel de France
hotel-france.ident: The Hotel de France stood at Bolshaya Morskaya 6, a block from the Red Arch.

kazan-bridge.name: Kazan Bridge, where the Nevsky crosses the Ekaterina Canal
kazan-bridge.ident: Reed’s “corner of the Ekaterina Canal” on the Nevsky: the Kazan Bridge, a short block west of the Duma. The canal is now the Griboyedov Canal.

kirochnaya-barracks.name: Barracks of the 6th Reserve Engineers, Kirochnaya
kirochnaya-barracks.ident: Reed lunches “in a courtyard on the Kirotchnaya” with the 6th Reserve Engineers’ Battalion; perhaps the Guards Sapper barracks. Not identified.

mariinsky-palace.name: Mariinsky Palace
mariinsky-palace.note: Seat of the Council of the Russian Republic (the Pre-Parliament) until it was dispersed on 7 Nov.

mikhailovskaya.name: Mikhailovskaya Street
mikhailovskaya.ident: “The Mikhailovsky” opposite the Duma: Mikhailovskaya Street, running north from the Nevsky.

mikhailovsky-manege.name: Mikhailovsky Riding School
mikhailovsky-manege.ident: The Mikhailovsky Manege, Manezhnaya Square, where the armoured-car troops were quartered.

military-hotel.name: Hotel Astoria (the “Military Hotel”)
military-hotel.ident: Reed’s “Military Hotel at the corner of St. Isaac’s Square”: the Astoria, used as the officers’ hotel during the war.

morskaya.name: Bolshaya Morskaya Street
morskaya.ident: Reed never says which Morskaya; the Telephone Exchange, the Hotel France and the Red Arch place his on the Bolshaya.

morskaya-nevsky.name: Corner of the Morskaya and the Nevsky
morskaya-nevsky.ident: The Bolshaya Morskaya meets Nevsky Prospekt by the Police Bridge.
morskaya-nevsky.reed: corner of the Morskaya and the Nevsky

moskovsky-gate.name: Moscow Triumphal Gate
moskovsky-gate.note: Dismantled in 1936 and set up again in 1958–61 from its castings.

nevsky-86.name: Nevsky 86
nevsky-86.ident: Reed: at Number 86 “we went through a passage into a courtyard, surrounded by tall apartment buildings”, to apartment 229. OSM addresses the plot as 84-86; the pin is in its courtyard block (литБ), behind the street front (way/60196034). Assumes the 1917 no. 86 lies within it.

palace-embankment.name: Palace Embankment, the Neva quay of the Winter Palace
palace-embankment.ident: Reed leaves the palace “through a door opening onto the Neva quay”: the embankment along its north front. Which door is not said, hence the radius.

pavlovsk-school.name: Pavlovsk Military School
pavlovsk-school.ident: The Pavlovsk school stood at Bolshaya Spasskaya (now Krasnogo Kursanta) 21 from 1887 (under that name from 1894), in the former Noble Regiment barracks, now used by the Mozhaysky Military Space Academy; not in the town of Pavlovsk. OSM has no no. 21: the pin is in the academy’s large building fronting the street between nos. 18 and 23 (addressed Pionerskaya 28), taken to be it.

post-office.name: Main Post Office
post-office.ident: The Main Post Office (Glavpochtamt) on Pochtamtskaya; Reed gives no address.

red-arch.name: The General Staff arch
red-arch.ident: Reed’s “Red Arch” is the arch of the General Staff building, then painted red, between Palace Square and the Morskaya.

reed-lodging.name: Reed’s lodging
reed-lodging.ident: Reed never gives the address. Walks that start or end “at home” start or end here, with no pin.
reed-lodging.reed: the Russian household where I lived

smolny.name: Smolny Institute
smolny.note: Seat of the Petrograd Soviet, the Tsay-ee-kah, the Military Revolutionary Committee, and from 8 Nov the Council of People’s Commissars.

smolny-hall.name: The great hall of Smolny
smolny-hall.note: The former ballroom where the Petrograd Soviet and the Second Congress met.

state-bank.name: State Bank
state-bank.ident: The State Bank in the former Assignation Bank, Sadovaya 21, on the Ekaterina Canal.

telegraph-agency.name: Petrograd Telegraph Agency (PTA)
telegraph-agency.ident: TASS’s history puts the PTA building on Pochtamtskaya (Post Office) Street; the house is not known, so the pin sits mid-street with a 200 m radius.

telephone-exchange.name: Central Telephone Exchange
telephone-exchange.ident: The city’s central telephone station, opened in 1905 at Bolshaya Morskaya 22.

uncle-toms-cabin.name: “Uncle Tom’s Cabin”, a traktir
uncle-toms-cabin.ident: Reed puts it across the street from Smolny’s gates; no address is known.

vladimir-school.name: Vladimir Military School
vladimir-school.addr1917: Malaya Grebetskaya 9 / Muzykantsky per. 5 / Bolshaya Grebetskaya 16
vladimir-school.ident: The Vladimir yunker school’s barracks, built 1899–1901, stood at Malaya Grebetskaya 9 (also Muzykantsky per. 5 and Pionerskaya 16); the pin is on the site, now mapped as Pionerskaya 16.
vladimir-school.today: Demolished in October 2007, except one small wing, for a commercial development.

alexandrovskaya.name: Alexandrovskaya station
alexandrovskaya.ident: The station west of Tsarskoye Selo on the Warsaw line.

pulkovo.name: Pulkovo and the Pulkovo heights
pulkovo.note: The ridge with the observatory, about 17 km south of the Winter Palace.

romanov-crossroads.name: The first cross-roads on the road “toward Romanov”
romanov-crossroads.ident: Reed’s truck ran some miles from Tsarskoye Selo “toward Romanov”; he was stopped at “the first cross-roads” and walked from there at dusk to the 2nd Tsarskoye Selo Rifles. Neither “Romanov” nor the cross-roads is identified.

tsarskoye-rifles-barracks.name: Barracks of the 2nd Tsarskoye Selo Rifles
tsarskoye-rifles-barracks.ident: Reed walks to their barracks “along the post-road”; not identified.

tsarskoye-soviet.name: The Tsarskoye Selo Soviet’s palace
tsarskoye-soviet.ident: Reed: the Soviet sat in “a wing of one of the Grand Ducal palaces”. Not identified; pinned in the town with a wide radius.
tsarskoye-soviet.reed: wing of one of the Grand Ducal palaces

tsarskoye-station.name: Tsarskoye Selo station
tsarskoye-station.today: The station building was destroyed in the Second World War; the present one is post-war.

brotherhood-grave.name: The Brotherhood Grave by the Kremlin wall

moscow-soviet.name: Moscow Soviet, the former Governor-General’s palace on Skobeliev Square
moscow-soviet.ident: The Moscow Soviet sat in the Governor-General’s palace on Skobeliev (now Tverskaya) Square.

moscow-station.name: Nikolaevsky Station, Moscow (now Leningradsky)
moscow-station.ident: The Moscow end of the Nicolai line.

nobles-club.name: Nobles’ Club (Assembly of the Nobility), now the House of the Unions, Moscow
nobles-club.ident: Reed’s “Dvorianskoye Sobranie--the Nobles’ Club”: the Moscow Assembly of the Nobility on Okhotny Ryad, requisitioned by the Moscow MRC on 14 November NS for the trade unions and renamed the House of the Unions.

bryant.name: Louise Bryant
bryant.note: Reed’s wife; he names her only in Chapter VIII, as an eyewitness of the St Isaac’s shooting.

holtzman.name: Holtzman
holtzman.note: Member of the Military Revolutionary Committee.

krasnov.name: General Pyotr Krasnov
krasnov.note: Commander of the Cossacks who marched on Petrograd for Kerensky.

lazimir.name: Pavel Lazimir
lazimir.note: Chairman of the Military Revolutionary Committee: “a tow-headed, eighteen-year-old boy”, in Reed’s words.

muraviov.name: Mikhail Muravyov
muraviov.note: Commander of the defence of Petrograd against Krasnov.

polkovnikov.name: Colonel Georgy Polkovnikov
polkovnikov.note: Commander of the Petrograd Military District; military chief of the yunker rising.

reed.name: John Reed
reed.note: The narrator. His lodging is never located: “the Russian household where I lived”.

trusishka.name: “Trusishka”, a Russian acquaintance of Reed’s
trusishka.note: Reed’s pseudonym for the man who got into Antonov’s car and would not be dislodged; Reed’s only source for the drive to the Narva Gate.

williams.name: Albert Rhys Williams
williams.note: American correspondent; Reed’s source for the siege of the Telephone Exchange.

committee-for-salvation.name: Committee for Salvation of Country and Revolution

council-of-republic.name: Council of the Russian Republic (the Pre-Parliament)

mossoviet.name: Moscow Soviet and its Military Revolutionary Committee

peasants-executive.name: Executive Committee of the All-Russian Peasants’ Soviets
peasants-executive.reed: Executive Committee of the Peasants’ Soviets

petrograd-soviet.name: Petrograd Soviet of Workers’ and Soldiers’ Deputies

tsay-ee-kah.name: The new Tsay-ee-kah elected by the Second Congress

tsay-ee-kah-old.name: The old Tsay-ee-kah (Central Executive Committee elected in June)

vikzhel.name: All-Russian Executive Committee of the Railway Workers’ Union (Vikzhel)

peter-paul-garrison.name: Garrison of the Peter and Paul Fortress

petrograd-cossacks.name: Cossack regiments of the Petrograd garrison

sailors.name: Sailors of the Baltic Fleet and Kronstadt

engineers-yunkers.name: Yunkers of the Nikolaevsky Engineering School

pavlovsk-yunkers.name: Yunkers of the Pavlovsk Military School

vladimir-yunkers.name: Yunkers of the Vladimir Military School

crowd.name: Crowds in the streets
crowd.note: Reed’s onlookers, passers-by and street crowds, drawn as townspeople; his words for them decide who they are.

duma-procession.name: The Duma’s procession to the Winter Palace
duma-procession.note: Councillors, Mensheviki and SRs from the Congress, and the Mayor, who set out to share the ministers’ fate on the night of 7 Nov.
duma-procession.reed: Going to die in the Winter Palace

events.title: A meeting at the Cirque Moderne
events.why: Reed dates it only to the weeks before the rising; the meetings were held at night.
events.sum: Across the river, in the bare amphitheatre of the Cirque Moderne, soldiers, sailors and workers pack the benches to hear a soldier from the front.
events.q: I went across the river to the Cirque Moderne, to one of the great popular meetings which occurred all over the city, more numerous night after night.

also.q: The bare, gloomy amphitheatre, lit by five tiny lights hanging from a thin wire, was packed from the ring up the steep sweep of grimy benches

pics.lic: Public domain: its photographer, Pirie MacDonald, died in 1942 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old-70-expired}}, {{PD-old-X-expired}})
pics.cap: John Reed in New York, about 1916, the year before he went to Russia.

events.title: Ten thousand at the Obukhov works
events.why: “One Sunday” in October; 28 Oct is a guess within the range, chosen only to order the scenes.
events.sum: One Sunday Reed rides a steam tram out along the Schlüsselburg Prospekt to a meeting of ten thousand at the Obukhov munitions plant; Lunatcharsky speaks.
events.q: ten thousand black-clothed men and women packed around a scaffolding draped in red, people heaped on piles of lumber and bricks, perched high upon shadowy girders

also.q: One Sunday we went, on a top-heavy steam tram that lumbered through oceans of mud, between stark factories and immense churches

pics.lic: Public domain: published before 1931 (US) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-1923}}, {{PD-US-expired}})
pics.cap: A machine shop of the Obukhov works in 1902, with the stem of a battleship on the floor: the works as a workplace, fifteen years before Reed’s meeting there.

events.title: Out to Smolny by streetcar
events.why: Undated; placed before the night session of 30 Oct only to order the scenes.
events.sum: Reed rides a crawling, jammed streetcar to the end of the line at Smolny, the Soviets’ headquarters “miles out on the edge of the city”.
events.q: Smolny Institute, headquarters of the Tsay-ee-kah and of the Petrograd Soviet, lay miles out on the edge of the city, beside the wide Neva.

also.q: I went there on a street-car, moving snail-like with a groaning noise through the cobbled, muddy streets, and jammed with people.

pics.lic: Public domain: printed in Petrograd in 1917 and in Reed’s book in 1919 (PD in Russia and the US)
pics.cap: Signs were posted up everywhere: "Comrades! For the sake of your health, preserve cleanliness!"

events.title: Trotzky denies an insurrection
events.why: “The night of October 30th”, New Style.
events.sum: At the Petrograd Soviet Trotzky calls the press’s talk of an armed rising an attempt “to discredit and wreck the Congress of Soviets”.
events.q: At a meeting of the Petrograd Soviet in Smolny, the night of October 30th, Trotzky branded the assertions of the bourgeois press

pics.lic: Public domain: published in A. R. Williams, Through the Russian Revolution (New York, 1921) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-US}})
pics.cap: Soldiers’ and workers’ deputies packed into a session of the Petrograd Soviet. Williams does not say which hall or when, so it may be the Tauride Palace before the Soviet moved to Smolny.
pics.by: Unknown; printed by A. R. Williams

events.title: The Day of the Petrograd Soviet
events.sum: Sunday 4 Nov is the Day of the Petrograd Soviet, with mass meetings all over the city; the Cossacks’ rival procession is called off.
events.q: Sunday, November 4th, was designated as the Day of the Petrograd Soviet, with immense meetings planned all over the city

pics.t: The Soviet’s appeal to the Cossacks
pics.lic: Public domain: a Soviet official document of 1917 (PD-RU-exempt), printed in Reed’s book in 1919 (PD in the US)
pics.cap: Appeal of the Petrograd Soviet to the Cosacks to call off their Krestny Khod—the religious procession planned for November 4th (our calendar).

events.title: The Council of the Republic
events.sum: Reed drops in on the Council of the Russian Republic, in bitter debate on Terestchenko’s foreign policy.
events.q: Monday morning, the 5th, I dropped in at the Marinsky Palace, to see what was happening in the Council of the Russian Republic.

pics.lic: Public domain: a photochrom published before 1906 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Detroit}}, {{PD-Switzerland-old-unknown}}, {{PD-US-expired}}, {{PD-two}})
pics.cap: St Isaac’s Square and, across it, the Mariinsky Palace, where the Council of the Republic sat. The colours are the printer’s, and the Astoria at the corner of the square was not yet built.

events.title: Yunkers on the Morskaya
events.sum: Outside, two companies of yunkers march up the Morskaya singing; at the corner of the Nevsky Reed buys Lenin’s pamphlet.
events.q: Two companies of yunkers passed swinging up the Morskaya … At the corner of the Nevsky I bought a pamphlet by Lenin

pics.lic: Public domain: a typographic cover too simple to be protected, published in 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-ineligible}}, {{PD-old-80-1923}}, {{PD-old-80-expired}}, {{PD-old-X-expired}}, {{PD-trivial}})
pics.cap: The pamphlet Reed bought at the corner of the Nevsky, “Will the Bolsheviki be Able to Hold the Power?”, as he gives its title: the cover of the first edition (Petrograd: Priboi, 1917).

events.title: A film by the Kazan Cathedral
events.why: After the twilight walk up the Nevsky and before Smolny, where Reed stays until three.
events.sum: Reed watches a bloody Italian film near the Kazan Cathedral; soldiers and sailors in front stare in wonder.
events.q: We went to a moving picture show near the Kazan Cathedral—a bloody Italian film of passion and intrigue.

events.title: Peter-Paul comes over
events.why: Reed “hurried to Smolny” after the film and left at three in the morning.
events.sum: In room 10 at Smolny, Lazimir of the Military Revolutionary Committee tells Reed the fortress garrison has joined them.
events.q: “Peter-Paul Fortress has just come over to us,” said he, with a pleased grin.

also.q: Amid cheers he announced that the Left Socialist Revolutionaries had agreed to send representatives into the Military Revolutionary Committee

pics.lic: Public domain: a Soviet official document of 1917 (PD-RU-exempt), printed in Reed’s book in 1919 (PD in the US)
pics.cap: Pass to Smolny Institute, issued by the Military Revolutionary Committee, giving me the right of entry at any time.

events.tp: at three o’clock in the morning
events.title: Guns at Smolny’s door
events.sum: Leaving Smolny, Reed sees two rapid-firing guns mounted at the door and patrols at the gates.
events.q: As I left Smolny, at three o’clock in the morning, I noticed that two rapid-firing guns had been mounted, one on each side of the door

pics.lic: Public domain: a Russian photograph whose term has run out (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Russia-expired}})
pics.cap: A Maxim gun on its wheeled mount at the top of Smolny’s entrance steps, with a soldier in a papakha and an armed man in a cap.

events.title: “We’re off!”
events.why: Shatov meets Reed on the steps as he leaves at three.
events.sum: Bill Shatov runs up the steps: the yunkers closed the Bolshevik papers, and Soviet troops have broken the government seals.
events.q: Kerensky sent the yunkers to close down our papers, Soldat and Rabotchi Put. But our troops went down and smashed the Government seals

events.title: Yunker batteries at the palace
events.why: After the morning papers, before Kerensky’s speech at the Mariinsky.
events.sum: Crossing Palace Square to the Foreign Office censor, Reed sees yunker artillery trot through the Red Arch and draw up before the Winter Palace.
events.q: As I crossed the Palace Square several batteries of yunker artillery came through the Red Arch at a jingling trot, and drew up before the Palace.

events.title: Kerensky’s last speech
events.why: The censor says Kerensky “had just gone” to the Council.
events.sum: Reed reaches the Council of the Republic at the end of Kerensky’s long speech of self-justification.
events.q: I hurried down to the Marinsky Palace, arriving at the end of that passionate and almost incoherent speech of Kerensky’s, full of self-justification and bitter denunciation of his enemies.

events.title: Cars turned out
events.why: After the Council’s vote, before nightfall at Smolny.
events.sum: At the corner of the Morskaya and the Nevsky soldiers stop private cars and send them to the Winter Palace; nobody knows whose soldiers they are.
events.q: At the corner of the Morskaya and the Nevsky, squads of soldiers with fixed bayonets were stopping all private automobiles, turning out the occupants, and ordering them toward the Winter Palace.

pics.t: An armoured car on the Morskaya
pics.lic: Public domain: published in The Times History of the War (London, 1918) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-US}})
pics.cap: Soldiers with an armoured car at a corner of the Morskaya, under the sign of the Marine Pharmacy. Commons has it from The Times History of the War (1918), as “Bolsheviks holding the end of a street with an armoured car”; no day is given.
pics.by: Unknown; printed in The Times History of the War

events.title: “Cronstadt is coming!”
events.why: Straight after the scene at the Morskaya corner.
events.sum: In front of the Kazan Cathedral, sailors with Avrora and Zaria Svobody on their hat bands tell the soldiers the fleet is coming.
events.q: On the sailors’ hat bands were Avrora and Zaria Svobody … One of them said, “Cronstadt is coming!”

pics.lic: Public domain: published in A. R. Williams, Through the Russian Revolution (New York, 1921) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-US}})
pics.cap: Armed sailors in peakless caps with cap tallies, bayonets fixed, above a crowd of soldiers in papakhas. Williams printed it as “Revolutionary sailors”, with no place or date.
pics.by: Unknown; printed by A. R. Williams

events.title: Night at Smolny
events.sum: The great hall fills for the old Tsay-ee-kah’s session, which is to welcome the Congress delegates; Dan, Trotzky and Martov speak.
events.q: As night fell the great hall filled with soldiers and workmen, a monstrous dun mass, deep-humming in a blue haze of smoke.

events.title: The Telegraph Agency occupied
events.sum: Reed’s chronology of the night: a detachment from Smolny takes the Petrograd Telegraph Agency.
events.q: At 1 A. M. a detachment of soldiers and sailors from Smolny occupied the Telegraph Agency.

moves.size: a detachment of soldiers and sailors

events.title: The Post Office occupied
events.sum: Reed’s chronology: the Main Post Office is occupied.
events.q: At 1.35 the Post Office was occupied.

events.title: The Bolsheviki walk out
events.why: Late in the night session, just before Reed meets Zorin “toward four”.
events.sum: When the old Tsay-ee-kah moves to take on the Congress’s functions, the Bolsheviki leave the hall and the resolution passes.
events.q: Whereupon all the Bolsheviki left the hall and the resolution was passed

events.title: What the papers said
events.why: Dien reports the night’s captures in the paper of the 7th; the time is that of the captures, which the control change dates, not of the reading.
events.sum: The paper Dien reports the night: the Bolsheviki have taken the Telephone Exchange, the Baltic Station and the Telegraph Agency.
events.q: Bolsheviki capture of the Telephone Exchange, the Baltic station, the Telegraph Agency

events.title: Kerensky at the Staff
events.sum: Reed’s chronology of 7 Nov: from four until dawn Kerensky stays at the Petrograd Staff Headquarters.
events.q: From 4 A. M. until dawn Kerensky remained at the Petrograd Staff Headquarters

events.title: “We’re moving!”
events.sum: Zorin, rifle on his shoulder, tells Reed ministers are arrested and regiments are marching on the Telephone Exchange, the Telegraph Agency and the State Bank.
events.q: Toward four in the morning I met Zorin in the outer hall … One regiment is on the march to capture the Telephone Exchange, another the Telegraph Agency, another the State Bank.

events.title: The Red Guard, and firing at the bridges
events.sum: On Smolny’s steps Reed first sees the Red Guard. Westward, rifle fire: yunkers trying to open the Neva bridges, sailors closing them.
events.q: On the steps of Smolny, in the chill dark, we first saw the Red Guard … Far over the still roofs westward came the sound of scattered rifle fire, where the yunkers were trying to open the bridges over the Neva

pics.lic: Public domain: its photographer, Yakov Steinberg, died in 1942 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Russia-expired}})
pics.cap: Soldiers in greatcoats and papakhas, one with a bandolier across his chest, and civilians in bowlers and caps, all armed, at the gates of the Smolny Institute.

events.title: The Military Hotel taken
events.sum: Reed’s chronology: “toward morning” the Military Hotel, the Astoria, is taken.
events.q: Toward morning the Military Hotel was taken

events.title: Arrests at the Staff
events.sum: At Peter-Paul an ensign of the Pavlovsky Regiment, on guard at the Staff that night, tells Reed how it began: arrests from half-past two, halted by Smolny, resumed after a run to Smolny, too late for most.
events.q: It was five o’clock when we got back to the Staff, and by that time most of them were gone.

also.q: A praporshtchik of the Pavlovsky regiment was telling us how the insurrection started.

events.title: The Telephone Exchange taken
events.why: Reed gives five o’clock; one minute later than the Military Hotel only to keep the two in his order.
events.sum: Reed’s chronology: at five the Telephone Exchange is taken.
events.q: and at 5 o’clock the Telephone Exchange

events.title: The Nicolai Bridge opened and shut
events.why: Three hours after an order given while Kerensky was at the Staff (from 4 a.m.).
events.sum: Three hours after Kerensky’s order to open the bridges, an officer and five men open the Nicolai Bridge; sailors close it again.
events.q: Kerensky gave an order to open the bridges; three hours passed without any action … opened the Nicolai Bridge. Immediately after they left, however, some sailors closed it again.

pics.lic: Public domain: a postcard published in the Russian Empire before 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}})
pics.cap: The Nicolai Bridge over the Neva, with the chapel on its swing span, on a postcard printed before 1917.

events.title: The State Bank surrounded
events.sum: Reed’s chronology: at dawn the State Bank is surrounded.
events.q: At dawn the State Bank was surrounded.

pics.lic: Public domain: a photogravure published in the early 1900s (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old-70-1923}}, {{PD-old-70-expired}}, {{PD-old-X-expired}})
pics.cap: Quarenghi’s State Bank seen across the Ekaterina Canal, in a photogravure of the early 1900s. Its main front is on the Sadovaya.

events.title: Kerensky leaves for the front
events.sum: Reed’s chronology: about nine Kerensky leaves the capital for the front.
events.q: About 9 A. M. Kerensky left for the Front

pics.lic: Public domain: its photographer, Karl Bulla, died in 1929 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}})
pics.cap: Alexander Kerensky, head of the Provisional Government, at his desk in 1917.

events.title: A cordon round the Winter Palace
events.sum: Reed’s chronology: at ten a cordon of troops is drawn about the Winter Palace.
events.q: And at 10 A. M. a cordon of troops was drawn about the Winter Palace.

events.title: “No more Government”
events.sum: Reed rises late. At noon, walking down the Nevsky, he asks the soldiers at the State Bank’s gates whose side they are on.
events.q: The noon cannon boomed from Peter-Paul as I went down the Nevsky. … “No more Government,” one answered with a grin, “Slava Bogu! Glory to God!”

events.title: Officers kept in the Military Hotel
events.why: After the State Bank and a talk with Gomberg at the Morskaya corner.
events.sum: Sailors picket the Military Hotel; the officers in its lobby are not allowed to leave.
events.q: The Military Hotel at the corner of St. Isaac’s Square was picketed by armed sailors.

events.title: The Council of the Republic dispersed
events.why: Straight after the Military Hotel: “I ran out.”
events.sum: Reed runs to the Mariinsky Palace at the sound of shots. A sailor tells how they turned the Council out.
events.q: Something unusual was going on around the Marinsky Palace

also.q: “We walked in there,” he said, “and filled all the doors with comrades.

events.title: Inside the besieged palace
events.why: After the Mariinsky, before “it was getting late”.
events.sum: Through the cordon by way of the Admiralteisky, on their American passports, Reed and others walk into the palace: a barracks of yunkers.
events.q: We went toward the Winter Palace by way of the Admiralteisky.

also.q: Machine guns were mounted on window-sills, rifles stacked between the mattresses.

pics.lic: Public domain: its photographer, Yakov Steinberg, died in 1942 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Russia-expired}})
pics.cap: A hall of the Winter Palace the day after its capture, the defenders’ mattresses and bedding heaped under the battle paintings.

events.title: A sortie through the Red Arch
events.why: Reed watches from a palace window, before dusk.
events.sum: Two companies of yunkers march off through the Red Arch, “to capture the Telephone Exchange”, and come back with their wounded.
events.q: went swinging off across the Square, disappearing through the Red Arch into the quiet city. … “They are going to capture the Telephone Exchange,” said some one.

also.q: For a while we stood at the window, looking down on the Square before the Palace

events.title: Dinner at the Hotel France
events.why: “It was getting late when we left the Palace.”
events.sum: At dinner the pale waiter moves them to the back room: the café lights are going out, “there will be much shooting”.
events.q: We went into the Hotel France for dinner, and right in the middle of soup the waiter, very pale in the face, came up and insisted that we move to the main dining-room at the back of the house

events.title: “The Women’s Battalion is in there”
events.why: After dinner, before the Police Bridge and the drive to Smolny.
events.sum: At the Red Arch soldiers stare at the lighted palace and argue against shooting.
events.q: “No, comrades,” one was saying. “How can we shoot at them? The Women’s Battalion is in there—they will say we have fired on Russian women.”

pics.lic: Public domain: published in E. A. Ross, The Russian Bolshevik Revolution (New York, 1921) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}})
pics.cap: Women soldiers in greatcoats and fur hats drawn up on Palace Square before the arch of the General Staff. Ross printed it in 1921 as the women’s Battalion of Death, without a date.
pics.by: Unknown; printed by E. A. Ross

events.title: A field-gun on the Nevsky
events.why: Back on the Nevsky after the Red Arch.
events.sum: In the dark the Police Bridge is barricaded with lumber, and soldiers wheel a three-inch field-gun into place before the Stroganov Palace.
events.q: In the darkness we stumbled over lumber-piles barricading the Police Bridge, and before the Stroganov Palace made out some soldiers wheeling into position a three-inch field-gun.

pics.t: The Nevsky from the Police Bridge
pics.lic: Public domain: a photochrom published in the 1890s (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})
pics.cap: The Nevsky seen from the Police Bridge over the Moika, toward the tower of the City Duma, in a photochrom of 1896–97, when the trams were still drawn by horses.

events.title: A red spark on a roof
events.why: The last scene before Smolny.
events.sum: Up the Nevsky, two thousand people at the Sadovaya corner stare at a red spark on a roof: “a provocator”, says a peasant.
events.q: On the corner of the Sadovaya about two thousand citizens had gathered, staring up at the roof of a tall building, where a tiny red spark glowed and waned.

events.title: The Second Congress opens
events.sum: Dan rings the bell to open the Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets.
events.q: It was 10.40 P. M. Dan, a mild-faced, baldish figure in a shapeless military surgeon’s uniform, was ringing the bell.

pics.lic: Public domain: its photographer, Yakov Steinberg, died in 1942 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Russia-expired}})
pics.cap: A Red Guard patrol warming itself at a fire on Smolny Prospekt, under a shop sign for icons.

events.title: The moderates walk out
events.why: Late in the opening session, before the MRC room and the truck.
events.sum: Abramovitch: the Bund joins the Mensheviki and SRs in leaving the Congress, to “perish with the Provisional Government”.
events.q: The Bund group joins with the declaration of the Mensheviki and Socialist Revolutionaries and will leave the Congress!

events.title: Men over a map
events.why: Just before Reed leaves Smolny on the truck.
events.sum: Through the door of the Military Revolutionary Committee Reed glimpses men bent over a map.
events.q: we caught a glimpse of dishevelled men bending over a map under the glare of a shaded electric-light

events.title: Proclamations from a truck
events.why: After the passes are made out at Smolny, before the Duma march.
events.sum: On an MRC truck Reed helps fling the proclamation of the Provisional Government’s fall into the streets, down the Suvorovsky and the Nevsky.
events.q: We imitated him, plunging down through the dark street with a tail of white papers floating and eddying out behind.

also.q: We turned into Znamensky Square, dark and almost deserted

pics.lic: Public domain: a Soviet official document of 1917 (PD-RU-exempt), printed in Reed’s book in 1919 (PD in the US)
pics.cap: I picked up a copy of the paper, and under a fleeting street-light read: TO THE CITIZENS OF RUSSIA!

events.title: The march to die in the Winter Palace
events.why: After the truck reaches the Duma, before the storming.
events.sum: The Duma, the Mayor and the Mensheviki and SRs set out to die with the ministers. Sailors stop them at the Ekaterina Canal, under 200 m from the Duma door, and they turn back.
events.q: “Going to die in the Winter Palace,” he shouted cheerfully.

also.q: “We will spank you!” he cried, energetically.

events.title: Through the Red Arch
events.why: Reed gives no hour for the entry; he leaves the palace “after three in the morning”.
events.sum: From the Morskaya Reed falls in with the column that pours through the Red Arch and across the square into the palace.
events.q: Like a black river, filling all the street, without song or cheer we poured through the Red Arch … jammed up suddenly behind the pedestal of the Alexander Column

also.q: the first two or three hundred men were Red Guards, with only a few scattered soldiers
Look out, comrades! Don't trust them. They will fire, surely!

moves.size: the first two or three hundred men were Red Guards

pics.lic: Public domain: a postcard published in the Russian Empire before 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}})
pics.cap: The General Staff and its arch, the “Red Arch” of Reed’s column, with the Alexander Column on Palace Square, on a postcard printed before 1917.

events.title: “Property of the People!”
events.why: Just after the entry.
events.sum: In the cellar the looting starts and is stopped by the crowd itself.
events.q: “Comrades! Don’t touch anything! Don’t take anything! This is the property of the People!”

pics.lic: Public domain: its photographer, Yakov Steinberg, died in 1942 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old-X-expired}}, {{PD-old-auto-expired}})
pics.cap: A room of the Winter Palace the day after its capture, papers strewn over the floor and the cupboards open. The photograph’s agency caption calls it the room of Grand Duchess Tatiana.

events.title: The ministers taken to Peter-Paul
events.why: “It was only later that we learned…”
events.sum: The arrested ministers are marched out; a crowd wants to lynch them, but the sailors get them to Peter-Paul.
events.q: the sailors brought them safely to Peter-Paul

pics.lic: Public domain: written in 1917 by A. I. Konovalov (died 1948) and first printed in Reed’s book in 1919 (PD in Russia and the US)
pics.cap: Facsimile of the beginning of a proclamation, written in pencil by A.I. Konovalov, Minister of Commerce and Industry in he Provisional Government, and then scratched out as the hopelessness of the situation became more and more evident.

events.title: The Women’s Battalion
events.why: Told on the quay as Reed leaves the palace, just before “It was now after three in the morning”.
events.sum: A Commissar tells Reed the women soldiers were found huddled in a back room, marched to the Finland Station and sent to their camp at Levashovo.
events.q: So finally we marched them up to the Finland Station and put them on a train for Levashovo, where they have a camp.

events.tp: It was now after three in the morning
events.title: Broken stucco
events.sum: Leaving the palace, Reed walks over stucco knocked off the cornice, “the only damage done by the bombardment”.
events.q: Underfoot the sidewalk was littered with broken stucco, from the cornice of the Palace where two shells from the battleship Avrora had struck … It was now after three in the morning.

pics.lic: Public domain: a Russian photograph whose term has run out (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Russia}})
pics.cap: A façade of the Winter Palace on the morning after the storming, the stone pocked and a window shot through.

pics.lic: Public domain: published in the Russian Empire before 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}}, {{PD-old}})
pics.cap: The cruiser Avrora at her moorings before the war: three funnels, two masts, a grey hull. No public-domain photograph of her in 1917 was found.

events.title: The Committee for Salvation is formed
events.why: Reed walks from the palace to the Duma “after three”.
events.sum: In the Duma’s Alexander Hall, on Skobeliev’s motion, the anti-Bolshevik groups form the Committee for Salvation of Country and Revolution.
events.q: We mounted to the galleried Alexander Hall … And as we looked on, the Committee for Salvation was formed

events.title: The Twelfth Army goes over
events.sum: Krylenko reads a telegram: the Twelfth Army’s new Military Revolutionary Committee has taken command of the Northern Front.
events.q: It was exactly 5:17 A.M. when Krylenko, staggering with fatigue, climbed to the tribune with a telegram in his hand.

also.q: he wanted thirty rubles, and stopped two blocks away

pics.lic: Public domain: published in 1918 (US) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-1923}}, {{PD-US-expired}})
pics.cap: Nikolai Krylenko at his desk before a wall map, in a news photograph of 1918.

events.title: The Internationalists leave
events.why: After Krylenko’s telegram at 5:17, before Reed leaves Smolny about six.
events.sum: Martov’s Menshevik Internationalists lose the vote on a peaceful settlement and leave the Congress “in a Whirlwind of Jocular insults”.
events.q: The vote was overwhelmingly against, and the Mensheviki Internationalists left the Congress in a Whirlwind of Jocular insults.

pics.lic: Public domain: its photographer, Yakov Steinberg, died in 1942 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Russia-expired}})
pics.cap: Julius Martov, leader of the Menshevik Internationalists, in Petrograd in 1917.

events.title: The Duma in permanence
events.sum: In the Nicolai Hall the Duma sits in permanence, gathering the opposition; Mayor Schreider describes his protest at Smolny.
events.q: In the high, amphitheatrical Nicolai Hall that afternoon I saw the Duma sitting in permanence, tempestuous, grouping around it all the forces of opposition.

pics.lic: Public domain: a photochrom published in the 1890s (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})
pics.cap: The City Duma and its clock tower on the Nevsky, in a photochrom of 1896–97. The colours are the printer’s.

events.title: Menshevik papers seized
events.why: Between the Duma that afternoon and the evening session at Smolny.
events.sum: At the corner of the Liteiny, Red Guards and sailors take a news-dealer’s Menshevik papers; an ugly crowd gathers.
events.q: Up on the corner of the Liteiny, five or six Red Guards and a couple of sailors had surrounded a news-dealer and were demanding that he hand over his copies of the Menshevik Rabot-chaya Gazeta

events.title: Lenin
events.sum: The presidium enters to a wave of cheers, Lenin among them. “We shall now proceed to construct the Socialist order!”
events.q: It was just 8.40 when a thundering wave of cheers announced the entrance of the presidium, with Lenin—great Lenin—among them.

also.q: “We shall now proceed to construct the Socialist order!”

pics.lic: Public domain: its photographer, Dmitry Leshchenko, died in 1937 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Russia}})
pics.cap: Lenin in hiding in August 1917, clean-shaven and in a wig for false papers. Reed saw him on 8 November “clean-shaven now, but already beginning to bristle with the well-known beard of his past and future”.

events.title: The proclamation on peace
events.sum: The Congress votes the proclamation to the peoples on peace; one hand goes up against and comes down again.
events.q: It was exactly 10:35 when Kameniev asked all in favour of the proclamation to hold up their cards.

pics.lic: Public domain: a Soviet official document of 1917 whose author died in 1924 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})
pics.cap: The Decree on Peace as printed for posting, “adopted unanimously” at the Congress session of 26 October, Old Style (8 November).
pics.by: V. I. Lenin, for the Congress of Soviets

events.title: The Land Decree
events.sum: The Land Decree passes with one vote against, the peasant delegates wild with joy.
events.q: At two o’clock the Land Decree was put to vote, with only one against and the peasant delegates wild with joy.

pics.lic: Public domain: a Soviet official document of 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RU-exempt}})
pics.cap: The front page of Izvestia for 10 November 1917 (28 October, Old Style), printing the Decree on Land.

events.title: The Council of People’s Commissars
events.sum: Kameniev reads the decree forming the Council of People’s Commissars.
events.q: At 2.30 A. M. fell a tense hush. Kameniev was reading the decree of the Constitution of Power

events.title: Home by the delegates’ tram
events.sum: Near seven, Reed rides home on the trams kept at Smolny for the delegates; at his apartment-house an armed citizens’ patrol stops them.
events.q: It was almost seven when we woke the sleeping conductors and motor-men … At our apartment-house we were held up in the dark by an armed patrol of citizens and carefully examined.

pics.lic: Public domain: published before 1931 (US) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old-70-1923}}, {{PD-old-70-expired}}, {{PD-old-X-expired}})
pics.cap: Cavalry under the banner of the 9th Reserve Cavalry Regiment ride along the Nevsky beside an electric tram, in the spring or summer of 1917.

events.title: At the Duma’s doors
events.why: Reed comes down the Nevsky in the late morning; the Duma is surrounded that afternoon.
events.sum: A handful of armed workers and soldiers come to seize the Duma’s papers and are mobbed by a well-dressed crowd shouting “Traitors!”
events.q: On one side a handful of workmen and common soldiers, with arms in their hands, representing a victorious insurrection—and perfectly miserable

events.title: An armoured car at the Duma
events.why: Between the scene at the doors and the Duma’s emergency session.
events.sum: After a Red Guard wounds a girl, an armoured car swings round the corner of the Mikhailovsky and the crowd throws itself down.
events.q: suddenly an armoured automobile appeared around the corner of the Mikhailovsky, its guns sluing this way and that.

also.q: A Red Guard, finally exasperated by the taunts of the crowd, had shot into it, wounding a young girl in the arm.

events.title: “It is all a mistake”
events.why: Before dusk, when the cyclists come down the Nevsky.
events.sum: The Duma, believing itself surrounded, sits in emergency session; Riazanov, Bolshevik councillor, says the troops will be withdrawn.
events.q: It is all a mistake. I told the Mayor this morning that the Duma would be left alone

events.title: Cyclists on the Nevsky
events.sum: At dusk a double file of cyclists, come from the front to back the Soviets, rides down the Nevsky and is surrounded by questioners.
events.q: Out on the Nevsky, in the deepening dusk, a long double file of cyclists came riding, guns slung on their shoulders.

events.title: “Will you give it back?”
events.why: After the cyclists at dusk, before Reed returns to the Duma.
events.sum: In the dim Mikhailovsky Riding School Krylenko, close to collapse, talks the two thousand armoured-car men out of neutrality.
events.q: The Government is in your hands. You are the masters. Great Russia belongs to you. Will you give it back?

events.title: Two commissions
events.why: Just before Reed reaches Peter-Paul at midnight.
events.sum: Back at the Duma, a commission goes with the Mayor to Peter-Paul to look into the yunkers’ treatment, and another is named to meet Kerensky.
events.q: As we followed them out, the Duma was appointing another commission to meet Kerensky

events.title: Into the fortress at midnight
events.sum: Reed bluffs his way into Peter-Paul behind the Duma’s commission, past the Tsars’ tombs, to the yunkers and the arrested ministers.
events.q: It was midnight when we bluffed our past the guards at the gate of the fortress

pics.lic: Public domain: a Soviet official document of 1917 (PD-RU-exempt), printed in Reed’s book in 1919 (PD in the US)
pics.cap: Pass from the Department of Prisons of the Soviet Government to visit freely all prisons of Petrograd and Cronstadt.

pics.lic: Public domain: a postcard published in the Russian Empire before 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})
pics.cap: The Peter and Paul Fortress across the Neva, its cathedral spire over the curtain wall, on a postcard printed before 1917.

events.title: A column to battle with Kerensky
events.why: “After-midnight”, on the way back from Peter-Paul.
events.sum: After midnight an endless column of soldiers shuffles up the Nevsky in silence, going to meet Kerensky.
events.q: Up the Nevsky, in the empty after-midnight gloom, an interminable column of soldiers shuffled in silence—to battle with Kerensky.

events.title: Bulletin from Krasnoye Selo
events.why: Posted after the 8 a.m. bulletin and before Reed leaves for Tsarskoye.
events.sum: At Smolny they paste up a bulletin from Krasnoye Selo calling Kerensky’s telegram false; the garrisons of Gatchina, Pavlovsk and Tsarskoye are falling back.
events.q: In the halls they were pasting up bulletins

events.title: The city pours out to dig trenches
events.why: The afternoon the trench order went out.
events.sum: At the order to dig trenches the factory whistles blow, and men, women and children stream through the slums toward the Moskovsky Gate.
events.q: South and southwest they poured through the shabby streets toward the Moskovsky Gate, men, women and children, with rifles, picks, spades, rolls of wire

events.title: Antonov inspects the trenches
events.why: Reed hears it from Trusishka, who went with them; Reed himself “made for the Tsarskoye Selo station”.
events.sum: Antonov and Dybenko drive from Smolny to the Narva Gate. A tyre bursts on the Nevsky, so they take an Italian-flagged taxi. A few hundred workmen wait in trenches for the Cossacks.
events.q: Arrived at Narvskaya Zastava, about ten miles out, Antonov called for the commandant of the Red Guard.

pics.t: Red Guards of the Putilov works
pics.lic: Public domain: its photographer, Yakov Steinberg, died in 1942 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Russia-expired}})
pics.cap: Red Guards of the Putilov works at rifle practice, in two ranks before a stack of logs. The Putilov works lay in the Narva district.

pics.lic: Public domain: published in A. R. Williams, Through the Russian Revolution (New York, 1921) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Scan}}, {{PD-old-100}})
pics.cap: Vladimir Antonov-Ovseenko of the Military Revolutionary Committee at his desk, as Williams printed him in 1921.
pics.by: Unknown; printed by A. R. Williams

events.tp: The early twilight of winter was falling
events.title: “Peace! Land!”
events.sum: On the way to the Tsarskoye Selo station Reed passes young Red Guards marching up the Nevsky under a gold-lettered red flag.
events.q: A red flag crudely lettered in gold, “Peace! Land!” floated over them. They were very young.

also.q: Heads up they tramped in the chill mud, irregular lines of four, without music, without drums.

pics.t: Reed’s pass to the Northern front
pics.lic: Public domain: a Soviet official document of 1917 (PD-RU-exempt), printed in Reed’s book in 1919 (PD in the US)
pics.cap: This pass was issued upon the recommendation of Trotzky three days after the Bolshevik Revolution. It gives me the right of free travel to the Northern front

events.title: Cannon heard at the Warsaw Station
events.why: The evening Reed came back from Tsarskoye.
events.sum: From the Warsaw Station, the railway toward Gatchina, a far-off cannonade can be heard.
events.q: From the Warsaw Railway station could be heard far-off cannonade.

pics.lic: Public domain: a postcard published in the Russian Empire before 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old-70}})
pics.cap: The Warsaw Station by the Obvodny Canal, on a postcard printed before 1917.

events.title: Cannonade heard in town
events.why: After the train back from Tsarskoye.
events.sum: Back in Petrograd, crowds surge up and down the Nevsky; from the Warsaw Station a distant cannonade can be heard.
events.q: Back in town excited throngs were moving in tides up and down the Nevsky.

also.q: From the Warsaw Railway station could be heard far-off cannonade.

events.title: A state of siege
events.why: Posted in the street as Reed leaves the Duma, the night of the 10th, just before “As we went home”.
events.sum: Podvoisky’s order declares Petrograd and its suburbs in a state of siege and forbids meetings in the open air.
events.q: are declared in a state of siege. All assemblies or meetings in the streets, and generally in the open air, are forbidden until further orders.

also.q: As we left the Duma a company of Red Guards

events.tp: In the small hours of the morning
events.title: Yunkers take the Telephone Exchange
events.sum: Before the guard changes, yunkers disguised as Semionovsky soldiers take the Telephone Exchange with the Bolshevik password, and capture Antonov.
events.q: In the small hours of the morning a company of yunkers, disguised as soldiers of the Semionovsky Regiment, presented themselves at the Telephone Exchange just before the hour of changing guard.

also.q: A few minutes later Antonov appeared, making a round of inspection. Him they captured and locked in a small room.
When the relief came it was met by a blast of rifle-fire, several being killed.

events.title: Ultimatum to the Vladimir school
events.sum: A patrol of soldiers, sailors and Red Guards gives the Vladimir yunkers twenty minutes to lay down their arms; they refuse.
events.q: At seven in the morning the Vladimir yunker school was visited by a patrol of soldiers, sailors and Red Guards, who gave the yunkers twenty minutes to lay down their arms.

pics.lic: Public domain: a postcard published in the Russian Empire before 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}})
pics.cap: The St Petersburg Infantry Junker School on an old postcard. Renamed the Vladimir Military School in 1910, it is very probably the building the Red Guards stormed on 11 November.

events.title: The yunkers strike in the city
events.sum: Petrograd wakes to rifle-fire: at dawn large forces of yunkers take the Military Hotel and the Telegraph Agency.
events.q: At dawn the Military Hotel and the Telegraph Agency had been taken by large forces of yunkers,

also.q: Petrograd woke to bursts of rifle-fire, and the tramping thunder of men marching.

events.title: The yunkers driven back
events.why: “An hour later” than the seven o’clock ultimatum.
events.sum: An hour after the ultimatum the Vladimir yunkers try to march out and are driven back by fire from the corner of the Grebetskaya and the Bolshoy Prospekt.
events.q: An hour later the yunkers got ready to march, but were driven back by a violent fusillade from the corner of the Grebetskaya and the Bolshoy Prospekt.

pics.t: Red Guards with an armoured car
pics.lic: Public domain: published in E. A. Ross, The Russian Bolshevik Revolution (New York, 1921) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-US}})
pics.cap: Red Guards firing from the snow beside a twin-turreted armoured car. Ross printed it in 1921 as a detachment of the Red Guard in a captured armoured car, without a place or a date.
pics.by: Unknown; printed by E. A. Ross

events.title: Bloodily recaptured
events.why: Reed gives no hour, only the order of events.
events.sum: The Military Hotel and the Telegraph Agency are retaken from the yunkers.
events.q: and bloodily recaptured.

events.title: The Telephone Station besieged
events.why: Reed’s account of the morning.
events.sum: Sailors besiege the Telephone Station from barricades of barrels and tin in the middle of the Morskaya and from the corners of the Gorokhovaya and St Isaac’s Square.
events.q: The Telephone Station was besieged by sailors, who lay behind barricades of barrels, boxes and tin sheets in the middle of the Morskaya

also.q: or sheltered themselves at the corner of the Gorokhovaya and of St. Isaac's Square, shooting at anything that moved

events.title: A Red Cross car
events.why: During the siege, before the storming in the afternoon.
events.sum: Williams, inside the Exchange, rides out in a Red Cross car “ostensibly full of wounded”, which goes by devious ways to the yunkers’ headquarters.
events.q: Albert Rhys Williams was in the Telephone Exchange. He went out with the Red Cross automobile, which was ostensibly full of wounded.

events.title: Field-guns at the Vladimir school
events.sum: Three field-pieces arrive; the yunkers shoot down two Soviet envoys under a white flag, and the bombardment begins.
events.q: At half-past eleven three field-pieces arrived.

also.q: Now began a real bombardment.

pics.lic: Public domain: a Russian photograph of 1916 whose term had run out by 1996 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Russia-1996}})
pics.cap: The Russian army’s 3-inch field-gun of 1902, with its crew, at the front in 1916.

events.title: Seven dead in an archway
events.why: During the day’s street fighting; no hour given.
events.sum: A yunker armoured car from the Admiralty stalls at the corner of the Gogolia and fires into the crowd; sailors swarm it with bayonets.
events.q: In the archway where Miss Bryant stood seven people were shot dead, among them two little boys.

also.q: As Louise Bryant was going along St. Isaac’s Square one came rolling up from the Admiralty, on its way to the Telephone Exchange.

events.title: The Vladimir school stormed
events.sum: The yunkers hoist a white flag; thousands pour in through windows and holes in the wall. Five yunkers are killed, about two hundred marched to Peter-Paul.
events.q: At half-past two the yunkers hoisted a white flag … With a rush and a shout thousands of soldiers and Red Guards poured through windows, doors and holes in the wall.

events.title: The Exchange stormed
events.why: “Until afternoon”.
events.sum: A Bolshevik armoured car arrives and the sailors storm the Exchange. Williams brokers Antonov’s release, and the yunkers go free.
events.q: The Telephone Exchange held out until afternoon, when a Bolshevik armoured car appeared, and the sailors stormed the place.

also.q: Williams offered to mediate if Antonov were released. This was immediately done

events.title: The last schools give up
events.why: “Two hours later” than the Vladimir surrender at half-past two.
events.sum: Two hours after the Vladimir school, the victors march on the Engineers’ Castle; the other schools surrender without a fight, and their yunkers go to Peter-Paul and Cronstadt.
events.q: Two hours later the Duma got a telephone message that the victors were marching toward the Injinierny Zamok … All the other schools surrendered without resistance

also.q: the yunkers were sent unharmed to Peter-Paul and Cronstadt

pics.lic: Public domain: a postcard published in the Russian Empire before 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}})
pics.cap: The Engineers’ Castle, home of the school of military engineers, behind trees on the Sadovaya, with electric trams, on a postcard printed before 1917.

events.title: Debate at the Kazan Cathedral
events.sum: At dusk on the almost empty Nevsky a crowd argues before the Kazan Cathedral: “To hell with Kerensky!”
events.q: On the almost deserted Nevsky, swept by a bitter wind, a crowd had gathered before the Kazan Cathedral, continuing the endless debate

pics.lic: Public domain: a photochrom published in the 1890s (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Detroit}}, {{PD-Switzerland-old-unknown}}, {{PD-US-expired}}, {{PD-two}})
pics.cap: The Kazan Cathedral and its colonnade on the Nevsky, in a photochrom of about 1896. The colours are the printer’s.

events.title: The Committee for Salvation outlawed
events.why: The evening after the rising was put down.
events.sum: At Smolny the Military Revolutionary Committee works without rest; new proclamations outlawing the Committee for Salvation litter the floor.
events.q: The Committee for Salvation had been outlawed.

events.title: Lenin and the regiments
events.sum: Lenin addresses delegates of the city regiments, who vote to fight and elect a staff of five.
events.q: At ten in the evening Lenin addressed a meeting of delegates from the city regiments, who voted overwhelmingly to fight.

events.tp: in the small hours of the morning
events.title: The regiments march out
events.sum: In the small hours the regiments leave their barracks for the front; Reed, going home, watches them pass.
events.q: Going home I saw them pass, swinging along with the regular tread of veterans, bayonets in perfect alignment, through the deserted streets of the conquered city

moves.size: the regiments left their barracks in full battle array

pics.lic: Public domain: published in A. R. Williams, Through the Russian Revolution (New York, 1921) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-US}})
pics.cap: Columns of soldiers with flags march down a Petrograd street, watched by women in headscarves. Williams printed it as battalions marching to Smolny; nobody wears winter dress, so it may be from before November.
pics.by: Unknown; printed by A. R. Williams

events.title: “We are perfectly neutral”
events.why: The day session, before dusk.
events.sum: Mayor Schreider tells the Duma it is neutral, and that he kept the telephones to Smolny working while the yunkers held the Exchange.
events.q: We are perfectly neutral. When the Telephone Exchange was occupied by the yunkers Colonel Polkovnikov ordered the telephones to Smolny disconnected

events.tp: By this time it was dusk
events.title: The Committee for Salvation in hiding
events.sum: A friend takes Reed to apartment 229 at Nevsky 86, where the hunted Committee for Salvation meets; Colonel Polkovnikov writes orders on the toilet.
events.q: At Number 86 Nevsky we went through a passage into a courtyard, surrounded by tall apartment buildings.

also.q: a heavily-built officer in a colonel’s uniform sat on the toilet, writing something on a pad held in his lap.

events.title: “Falling back from Krasnoye Selo”
events.why: After dusk at Nevsky 86, by streetcar to Smolny.
events.sum: At the Petrograd Soviet Trotzky reports: the Cossacks fall back from Krasnoye Selo, heavy fighting at Pulkovo, and the Kremlin in the yunkers’ hands.
events.q: The Cossacks are falling back from Krasnoye Selo.

also.q: At Pulkovo heavy fighting is going on. All available forces must be hurried there

pics.lic: Public domain: a Bain News Service photograph, published before 1931 (US) (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-Bain}}, {{PD-old-70-1923}}, {{PD-old-70-expired}}, {{PD-old-X-expired}})
pics.cap: Trotsky at his desk, in a news photograph probably of 1918: the military tunic suggests his time as Commissar for War, after these days.

events.tp: almost three o’clock in the morning
events.title: “Kerensky is smashed!”
events.sum: Leaving the hall, Reed is met by Holtzman of the MRC, who reads out a pencilled telegram from the Pulkovo staff. It is dated in the Old Style.
events.q: It was almost three o’clock in the morning when, as we left the hall, Holtzman, of the Military Revolutionary Committee, came running down the hall with a transfigured face.

doc.q: Pulkovo. Staff. 2.10 A.M. The night of October 30th to 31st will go down in history.

events.title: A train for the sailors
events.why: Straight after the telegram, by car across Znamensky Square.
events.sum: At the Nicolai Station Vikzhel’s men refuse to carry sailors to Moscow, until a few railwaymen open a door: “This way, comrades!”
events.q: “This way, comrades!” cried one. “We will take you to Moscow—or Vladivostok, if you like! Long live the Revolution!”

pics.lic: Public domain: a postcard published in the Russian Empire before 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}})
pics.cap: The Nicolai Station on Znamensky Square, on a postcard from the days of the horse tram.

events.title: First snow
events.sum: Early in the morning, walking up to Smolny, Reed sees the first snow: “Good for the health!” says the soldier at the door.
events.q: Going up the long wooden sidewalk from the outer gate I saw the first thin, hesitating snow-flakes fluttering down from the grey, windless sky.

pics.t: The order to send Reed’s despatch
pics.lic: Public domain: a Soviet official document of 1917 (PD-RU-exempt), printed in Reed’s book in 1919 (PD in the US)
pics.cap: Order given me at Staff headquarters by command of the Council of People’s Commissars, to transmit the first despatch out of Perograd after the November Revolution

pics.lic: Public domain: a postcard published in the Russian Empire before 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}})
pics.cap: The Smolny Institute across its square in snow, on a postcard printed before 1917.

events.title: Volunteers at the ledgers
events.why: Between Smolny in the early morning and Smolny about noon.
events.sum: At the State Bank the new Commissar, Petrovitch, and sweating volunteer soldiers and sailors try to make sense of the ledgers the striking clerks left.
events.q: I went to the State Bank to see the new Commissar, a redhaired Ukrainean Bolshevik named Petrovitch.

pics.t: A leaflet sold in the streets
pics.lic: Public domain: printed in Petrograd in 1917 and in Reed’s book in 1919 (PD in Russia and the US)
pics.cap: Popular leaflet sold in the streets just after the Bolshevik insurrection, containing rhymes and jokes about the defeated bourgeoisie and the "moderate" Socialist leaders

events.title: An ambulance for the front
events.sum: About noon Reed gets a ride in a volunteer ambulance bound for the revolutionary front.
events.q: About noon I was again in front of Smolny, talking with the driver of an ambulance bound for the revolutionary front.

events.title: Lunch with the Engineers
events.why: After “about noon” at Smolny.
events.sum: The ambulance stops for lunch with the committee of the 6th Reserve Engineers’ Battalion in a barracks courtyard on the Kirochnaya.
events.q: On the Kirotchnaya we turned into an immense courtyard surrounded by military buildings

events.title: The road to the front
events.why: After lunch, on the way to Pulkovo.
events.sum: Down the Liteiny and the Zagorodny and under the Moskovsky Gate; the highway is thronged with Red Guards going out and coming back.
events.q: It was thronged with Red Guards, stumbling along on foot toward the revolutionary front, shouting and singing; and others, greyfaced and muddy, coming back.

also.q: Straight down the Liteiny we rattled, and along the Zagorodny Prospekt.

pics.lic: Public domain: a postcard published in the Russian Empire before 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}})
pics.cap: The Moscow Triumphal Gate, Reed’s “Moskovsky Gate”, on the road south out of the city, on a postcard printed before 1917. It was taken down in 1936 and rebuilt after the war.

events.title: Trains “southwest” to Moscow
events.why: “For the past week”, written of the days before Reed’s own trip to Moscow.
events.sum: For a week the MRC and the railwaymen have held the Nicolai Railroad and sent train after train of sailors and Red Guards toward Moscow.
events.q: For the past week the Petrograd Military Revolutionary Committee, aided by the rank and file of the Railway Workers, had seized control of the Nicolai Railroad, and hurled trainload after trainload of sailors and Red Guards southwest

moves.size: trainload after trainload of sailors and Red Guards

events.title: The Red Guards come home
events.sum: Two thousand Red Guards march down the Zagorodny Prospekt behind a band playing the Marseillaise, home from defending Red Petrograd.
events.q: On the evening of November 16th I watched two thousand Red Guards swing down the Zagorodny Prospekt behind a military band playing the Marseillaise

also.q: with blood-red flags over the dark ranks of workmen

pics.t: The Red Guard of the Vulkan works
pics.lic: Public domain: its photographer, Viktor Bulla, died in 1938 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})
pics.cap: The Red Guard of the Vulkan works under its banner, with a Maxim and a Colt machine gun.

events.title: The press decree crisis
events.why: “The night of November 17th”.
events.sum: At a packed and ominous Tsay-ee-kah, Bolsheviks attack the press decree; Lenin wins the vote, the Left SRs quit the Military Revolutionary Committee, and five Commissars resign.
events.q: On the night of November 17th the great hall was packed and ominous for the meeting of the Tsay-ee-kah.

pics.lic: Public domain: a Soviet official document of 1917 (PD-RU-exempt), printed in Reed’s book in 1919 (PD in the US)
pics.cap: Announcement, posted on the walls of Petrograd, of the result of a meeting of representatives of the garrison regiments, called to consider the question of forming a new Government.

events.title: “Uncle Tom’s Cabin”
events.why: An evening after the snow came; one Red Guard speaks of “last Sunday”, so probably the week after 11 Nov.
events.sum: One evening in a Red Guards’ traktir across from Smolny’s gates, an officer argues politics with the Red Guards at the tea tables.
events.q: I sat one evening in a traktir--a kind of lower-class inn--across the street from the gates of Smolny; a low-ceilinged, loud place called “Uncle Tom’s Cabin,” much frequented by Red Guards.

events.tp: About seven o’clock in the evening
events.title: The train to Moscow
events.why: Reed gives the hour, not the day. He decided to go once the Kremlin had been Bolshevik “for two days” (it surrendered on the 15th), and the Commissars who had just resigned were on the train: so the 17th at the earliest. The 19th is an estimate; Reed gives no date.
events.sum: About seven in the evening Reed’s train pulls out of the Nicolai Station, drawn by a weak wood-burning engine, with soldiers on the roof and debates in the corridors.
events.q: About seven o’clock in the evening we drew out of the station, an immense long train drawn by a weak little locomotive burning wood

events.title: The Peasants’ Congress opens
events.why: “By November 23d about four hundred had gathered”; the first session followed.
events.sum: The Extraordinary Peasants’ Congress meets in the Duma’s Alexander Hall: more than half Left SRs, a fifth Bolsheviki, a quarter conservative SRs.
events.q: The first session took place in the Alexander Hall of the Duma building

events.title: The peasants make terms
events.sum: After an all-night struggle in the secret conferences at Smolny, the Left SRs and the Bolsheviki agree: the Tsay-ee-kah is to be doubled by 108 members from the Peasants’ Congress, plus delegates of the Army, the Fleet and the Trade Unions.
events.q: Wednesday morning, November 28th, after a terrible all-night struggle, an agreement was reached.

also.q: a series of secret conferences were already going on between the Left Socialist Revolutionaries and the Bolsheviki at Smolny

events.title: Tchernov leaves the hall
events.why: The session at Fontanka 6 that Reed dates “on Wednesday afternoon”, after the morning’s agreement.
events.sum: At Fontanka 6 Tchernov goes between the Congress and the old Executive’s rump meeting; when he warns the Congress against the agreement, laughter drives him from the platform and the room.
events.q: He was interrupted by a great burst of laughter; and realising the situation, he left the platform and the room, taking his popularity with him....

pics.lic: Public domain: published in the Russian Empire before 7 November 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-RusEmpire}})
pics.cap: Victor Chernov (Reed’s Tchernov), leader of the Socialist Revolutionaries, photographed in Petrograd in 1917, when he was a minister.

events.title: A holiday feeling
events.sum: The Congress meets in extraordinary session in a holiday mood. Reed dates it “Thursday, November 16th”, an Old Style date (= 29 Nov), just after a New Style “November 28th”.
events.q: Late in the afternoon of Thursday, November 16th, the Congress met in extraordinary session.

also.q: There was a holiday feeling in the air; on every face was a smile

events.title: The torchlit march to Smolny
events.sum: Out of the building in the dark: the Pavlovsky Regiment’s band plays the Marseillaise, banners unfurl, and the peasants march with torches down the bank of the Fontanka to Smolny.
events.q: From somewhere torches appeared, blazing orange in the night, a thousand times reflected in the facets of the ice, streaming out smokily over the throng as it moved down the bank of the Fontanka singing

also.q: Along the bank of the canal were drawn up in full marching order the soldiers of the Pavlovsky Regiment, with their band, which broke into the Marseillaise.
So the great procession wound through the city, growing and unfurling ever new red banners lettered in gold.

say: Long live the union of the revolutionary and toiling masses!
We bow to this flag in order to create the brotherhood of all people!

pics.lic: Public domain: a postcard published in the Russian Empire before 1917 (Wikimedia Commons: {{PD-old}})
pics.cap: The Imperial School of Jurisprudence on the Fontanka, Fontanka 6, where the Peasants’ Soviet sat, on a postcard printed before 1917.

events.title: Two banners on one wall
events.why: On the procession’s arrival.
events.sum: In Smolny’s hall the two presidiums embrace, the two banners are hung together over the empty frame of the Tsar’s portrait, and the “triumphal session” opens.
events.q: behind them the two banners were intertwined against the white wall, over the empty frame from which the Tsar’s picture had been torn

events.title: The Duma turned out
events.why: Reed gives the date, not the hour.
events.sum: At the Duma’s meeting of 2 December an officer and sailors walk into the Nicolai Hall and order the members out; they go, “ceding to violence”.
events.q: At the meeting of December 2d, an officer and some sailors entered the Nicolai Hall while a member was speaking, and ordered the members to leave, or force would be used.
